section.title: Final Warnings and Benediction
section.sectionRationale: The letter closes with warning and grace held together. Paul comes a third time, and every matter will be settled by two or three witnesses; he will not spare the unrepentant, for Christ who was crucified in weakness now speaks powerfully through him. He turns the test back on the church, Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith, then prays for their restoration, and ends with the fullest trinitarian blessing in his letters: the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit.
section.thesis: Christ crucified in weakness yet living by God's power is the pattern for both apostolic authority and the believer's life, so the church must examine itself, aim for restoration, and live in the grace of the triune God.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the final warning established by witnesses and grounded in the crucified yet living Christ; the call to self-examination and the prayer for restoration; and the closing appeal with the trinitarian benediction.

units.label: Established by witnesses
units.note: crucified in weakness, living by God's power

verses.text: This is the third time I am coming to you. “Every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.”
I already warned you the second time I was with you. So now in my absence I warn those who sinned earlier and everyone else: If I return, I will not spare anyone,
since you are demanding proof that Christ is speaking through me. He is not weak in dealing with you but is powerful among you.
For He was indeed crucified in weakness, yet He lives by God's power. For we are also weak in Him, yet by God's power we will live with Him concerning you.

units.label: Examine yourselves
units.note: test whether you are in the faith

verses.text: {{dokimazo|Examine}} yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves. Do you not realize that Jesus Christ is in you, unless you fail the test?
And I hope you will realize that we have not failed the test.
Now we pray to God that you will not do anything wrong, not that we will appear to have stood the test, but that you will do what is right, even if we appear to have failed.
For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.
In fact, we rejoice when we are weak but you are strong, and our prayer is for your {{katartisis|perfection}}.
This is why I write these things while absent, so that when I am present I will not need to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord gave me for building you up, not for tearing you down.

units.label: The grace of the triune God
units.note: aim for restoration, live in peace

verses.text: Finally, brothers, rejoice! Aim for perfect harmony, encourage one another, be of one mind, live in peace. And the God of love and peace will be with you.
Greet one another with a holy kiss.
All the saints send you greetings.
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the {{koinonia|fellowship}} of the Holy Spirit be with all of you.

dokimazo.gloss: To examine, to test, to prove by trial as metal is assayed. Paul turns the Corinthians' demand for proof of his apostleship back upon themselves: they are to test whether they are in the faith. The related word for passing or failing the test runs through the passage. The aim is not morbid doubt but honest self-scrutiny that leads to assurance that Jesus Christ is in the believer.

katartisis.gloss: Restoration, mending, being put into full order, as a broken bone is set or a torn net is repaired. Paul's prayer is for the Corinthians' restoration, their being brought to completeness and maturity. The related verb appears again in the appeal to aim for perfect harmony. The word joins the mending of what is broken with the reaching of what is intended, a fitting hope for a divided church.

koinonia.gloss: Fellowship, sharing, communion, participation together in something held in common. In the closing blessing the fellowship of the Holy Spirit is the shared life the Spirit creates among believers and between them and God. It is not mere friendliness but genuine partaking in the life of God, binding the church into one body and drawing it into the love of the Father and the grace of the Son.

basic.context: Paul draws the letter to a close with a firm warning and a tender blessing. Coming a third time, he says every charge will be settled by two or three witnesses, and he will not spare the unrepentant, for the Christ who speaks through him is not weak but powerful. He then turns the tables: instead of testing him, the Corinthians should examine themselves to see whether they are truly in the faith, with Christ in them. He prays for their restoration and ends with the great threefold blessing of grace, love, and fellowship.
basic.hermeneutics: Hold the warning and the grace together; the letter ends with both. The key move is in verse 4, where Christ crucified in weakness yet living by God's power becomes the pattern for Paul's ministry and for the church. Read Examine yourselves not as a recipe for endless anxiety but as a call to honest self-testing that ends in assurance. The trinitarian benediction gathers the whole letter into the life of the triune God.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul calls them to dokimazo, to test and prove themselves, the very examination they had demanded of him. His prayer is for their katartisis, their restoration and mending into full order. And the blessing ends with the koinonia of the Holy Spirit, the shared communion the Spirit creates with God and with one another.
basic.typology: The rule of two or three witnesses is drawn straight from the law of Moses, now applied in the church. Christ crucified in weakness yet raised in power fulfills the pattern glimpsed throughout Scripture, that God brings life through apparent defeat. The prayer for restoration echoes the prophets' longing for a mended people, fulfilled as Christ puts His body together in maturity.
basic.christ: Christ is the center of the closing. He was crucified in weakness yet lives by God's power, and this is both the ground of Paul's authority and the shape of the believer's life. The test of true faith is whether Jesus Christ is in you. And the benediction begins with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every other blessing flows, revealing the Son as one with the Father and the Spirit.
basic.god: The passage ends on the triune God: the grace of the Son, the love of the Father, and the fellowship of the Spirit. God is the God of love and peace who dwells with a reconciled people. He is the source of the power by which Christ lives and by which Paul serves, and He gives authority for building up rather than tearing down. The whole letter closes inside the life of this God.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 19 gives the rule of two or three witnesses. Matthew 28 shows the triune name in baptism. 1 Corinthians 11 uses the same call to self-examination before the Lord's table.
basic.oneStory: The Bible moves from a world fractured by sin to a people restored and dwelling with God. Here the letter ends by pressing the church to examine itself, aim for restoration, and live in peace, all within the grace of Father, Son, and Spirit. Christ crucified in weakness and living in power is the hinge, and the triune blessing points to the communion with God that is the goal of the whole story.

context.literary:
Chapter 13 is the last of three panels that close the letter. Chapters 10 to 12 argued the case for Paul's apostleship against rivals who measured leaders by polish and power. Chapter 13 turns from argument to verdict, and it is built as a sequence of reversals. The Corinthians have been sitting as judges of Paul, demanding proof, verse 3. By verse 5 the bench has been turned around and they are the ones under examination. Paul has been called weak, and in verse 4 he accepts the word and sets it beside Christ Himself. He has been accused of a heavy hand, and in verse 10 he says he is writing precisely so that his hand need not fall.

The first four verses move by a pattern of threes. This is the third visit, verse 1, and the law of the witnesses is quoted to match it. A warning given on the second visit is repeated in absence, verse 2. Then comes a hinge, verse 4, built on a double 'indeed ... yet' that is repeated for Christ and for the apostles: crucified in weakness, living by God's power; weak in Him, living with Him by that power. Everything after rests on this verse.

Verses 5 to 10 are a run of short, almost clipped sentences, with the word for testing or passing the test recurring again and again. The repetition makes the section feel like a hand pressed against the Corinthians' conscience. In verses 7 to 9 Paul weaves together three clauses that sound contradictory until they are heard together: he prays that they do right even if he looks like a failure, he cannot act against the truth, and he rejoices to be weak if they are strong.

Then the letter changes register at verse 11. The word 'finally' opens a string of five quick imperatives, a kiss, greetings from all the saints, and the benediction. The closing is the only place in Paul's letters where grace, love and fellowship are set out in this threefold form, and it leaves the argument of the whole letter standing inside a prayer.
context.historical:
Paul is writing, most likely from Macedonia, a few months before he reaches Corinth for the last time. Luke tells us that he spent three months in Greece, Acts 20:2-3, and it was during that stay that he wrote to the Romans. By the time of this letter the church had already given him a great deal of grief. He had planted it on his first visit, Acts 18, had written at least one earlier letter, and had made what he calls a 'painful visit', 2 Corinthians 2:1, which he did not want to repeat. The 'third time' of 13:1 is the visit he announces in 12:14, so 'third' counts the visit he is about to make, not one that has happened.

The quoted rule comes from the law of Moses, Deuteronomy 19:15, which was meant to protect an accused person from a single malicious voice. By the first century it had passed into Jewish legal practice and Jesus applied it to the settling of disputes between believers, Matthew 18:16. Paul does not mean that he will conduct a trial with two or three outside witnesses. The sense is that the rule's spirit governs the case: nothing will be done on rumour, and each charge will be tested before it is judged. Some readers have taken the three visits and the warnings as the witnesses themselves, and Paul's careful rehearsal of earlier warnings in verse 2 would fit that.

The Corinthians lived in a Roman colony and a port city that prized rhetoric, status and visible success. In such a place, the claim that a leader is weak counted as a disqualification, and the rival apostles of chapters 10 to 12 had fed on it. Paul's reply is that the crucified Messiah Himself looked weak. The greetings in verses 12 and 13 reflect the practice of the early house churches: they met in homes, welcomed one another with a kiss, and carried greetings from the other communities on the road. The 'saints' who send greetings were likely the Macedonian believers around Paul.
context.canonical:
The rule of witnesses begins in the law, Deuteronomy 17:6 and 19:15, and runs through the whole Bible. Jesus uses it in the Gospel of John to say that the Father and He together make two testimonies, John 8:17. The church applies it to elders, 1 Timothy 5:19, and the letter to the Hebrews recalls its severity under Moses, Hebrews 10:28. Paul's use sits between the courtroom and the congregation: it protects the accused while insisting that sin be named.

The call to test oneself has deep roots. Israel's wilderness years were a testing to find out what was in their heart, Deuteronomy 8:2. The psalmist asks God to search and test him, Psalm 139:23-24, and Lamentations turns the sentence into a corporate summons, 'Let us examine and test our ways, and turn back to the LORD,' Lamentations 3:40. At the Lord's Supper Paul has already asked each believer to examine himself, 1 Corinthians 11:28, and John tells the church to test the spirits, 1 John 4:1. The Corinthians' demand to test Paul is thus turned back on them in a form Scripture had long sanctioned.

The strength through weakness of verse 4 is a thread Paul has pulled throughout the letter: the treasure in jars of clay, 4:7-12, and the word the Lord spoke to him, 'My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness,' 12:9. It also recalls the way he first came to Corinth, 'in weakness and fear, and with much trembling,' 1 Corinthians 2:3, and the whole argument about the cross as the power of God, 1 Corinthians 1:23-25.

The ending belongs to a family of Pauline benedictions. Grace is the first word of every letter and, with few exceptions, the last. The threefold shape is the closest he comes to a formula, and it lines up with the structure of Matthew 28:19, Ephesians 4:4-6 and 1 Peter 1:2. Revelation, the last book, also ends on grace, Revelation 22:21.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wanted the Corinthians to hear two things at once and refuse to choose between them. First, that he was serious. He had already warned them twice, and he was ready to act with the authority the Lord gave him. Love that never disciplines was not the love he had for them. Second, that he did not want to use that authority at all. He says in verse 10 that this very letter is meant to spare them the visit he would otherwise have to make, so that his authority is spent on building up rather than tearing down.

Behind that lies a more pointed aim. The Corinthians had been testing whether Christ really spoke through him. Paul does not defend himself with credentials. He shows that the test they were applying to him was the wrong way round. If they were really in Christ, the proof of his apostleship was standing in front of them, because the church itself was his work, as he had said in 1 Corinthians 9:1-2. If they failed, the problem was their own, not his.

He also wanted them to recognise that the real danger was not his reputation but their drift. Verses 7 to 9 say it plainly. He is not praying for his own vindication. He is praying that they will do what is right, even if he looks like the loser. An apostle who is content to appear to have failed, provided his people are made whole, is the opposite of the boasting rivals.

Finally, he meant the letter to end in hope. The imperatives of verse 11, the greeting and the benediction invite a church under strain to receive the grace they need before they have fixed anything. Repair and reconciliation come from that grace, not before it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records Paul's plan, his warning and his prayer, and it contains a handful of direct commands: examine yourselves, rejoice, aim for harmony, encourage one another, live in peace, greet one another. The commands to the whole church bind believers in every age. The remark about coming a third time and sparing no one is a statement of Paul's own intention as an apostle, and it should not be copied as a pattern for leaders today who would speak in that tone. Whatever authority a church leader has is derivative, and Paul himself limits it in verse 10.

The holy kiss is a custom that records the way first century believers showed welcome. The command underneath it, to greet one another as family, is permanent, and the form is cultural. Many churches keep a handshake, an embrace or a greeting of peace for the same reason. The lesson is that fellowship must be bodily and visible, not merely stated.

The call to self-examination needs care. It is a command to the church to look at its own life in the light of Christ, not an instruction to dig for proof of salvation by studying one's feelings. Used rightly, it is a practice of repentance that leads to assurance.

debates.question: What does 'Jesus Christ is in you' mean in verse 5?

views.label: Christ dwelling in each believer by the Spirit
views.case: The wording is plural and the test is one each believer can apply to the self. Paul elsewhere says the Christian life is Christ in the believer, Galatians 2:20, and Romans 8:9-10 treats the Spirit's indwelling as the very mark of belonging to Christ. On this reading the examination looks for the Spirit's presence, shown in faith and in a changed life.

views.label: Christ present among the church as a body
views.case: The Greek preposition can be rendered 'among', and the whole section concerns the church as a community that has been tempted to dismiss the Lord's own speaker. Christ among them would then be proved by the unity, repentance and holiness of the congregation, as in the picture of Ephesians 2:21-22.

debates.bearing: The two readings are not rivals, since Paul's own theology holds that Christ dwells in each believer and among believers together. What matters is that the test is Christ, not Paul's reputation, and not the strength of anyone's feelings.

debates.question: Is the examination meant to unsettle believers or to assure them?

views.label: A warning that some may have an empty profession
views.case: The final clause, 'unless you fail the test,' admits that failure is possible. Paul also fears, in 12:20 and 12:21, that unrepented sin remains among them. Some in the Reformed tradition have drawn on this verse and on 2 Peter 1:10 to say that believers should make their calling and election sure.

views.label: A call to confident recognition
views.case: The wording expects a positive result: 'Can't you see for yourselves that Jesus Christ is in you' and his hope in verse 6 is that they will find he has not failed. The question assumes the answer yes, and the aim is a settled assurance that rests on Christ.

debates.bearing: Both are right in their place. Paul writes with a real warning and an expectant hope. A believer who finds Christ in the creed, the confession and the repentance of the heart is meant to be steadied, and one who finds nothing is meant to be roused. The test is always about Christ, never about how much the self has achieved.

debates.question: Is the 'third visit' a real third visit or an intended one?

views.label: An announced visit still to come
views.case: Paul says he is 'ready to come a third time' in 12:14 and speaks in the present of 'this is the third time I am coming'. The second visit was the painful one, 2:1, and the first was the founding visit of Acts 18.

views.label: A visit already made but not recorded
views.case: Some have thought Paul had made two visits in the past before this letter, or that a short third had occurred, because the language of the witnesses sounds retrospective. Luke does not record a second visit before this one.

debates.bearing: Most readers prefer the first. Either way the point stands: Paul has repeated his warning enough to satisfy the standard of a matter 'established,' and what follows is up to the church.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb of the central verse is dokimazo, which means to test in order to approve, as a metal is assayed. In verse 5 Paul pairs it with a second verb, peirazo, to put to the proof, and says 'examine' and 'test' of the self in two tight clauses. The pairing is not accidental. Peirazo can mean to tempt as well as to test, and dokimazo carries the hope of a pass. Together they invite an honest inquest that is not a hunt for guilt. The noun that goes with it, adokimos, means 'failed the test' or 'disqualified,' and it recurs three times in verses 5 to 7. In verse 5 it is a possibility for the Corinthians, in verse 6 Paul hopes they will recognise that he has not failed, and in verse 7 he is willing to look as though he had. He turns the word over until its meaning is exposed: proof matters, but it is Christ's proof, not social approval.

The clause 'Do you not realize' uses the verb epiginosko, to know fully or recognise. The Corinthians had been asking for evidence, and Paul says the evidence is already within reach if they would only recognise what they are. The same verb is used elsewhere for knowing by close acquaintance, and it fits the picture of a church that has not yet taken stock of what it has received.

Verse 4 uses a pair of prepositions that sound alike in Greek, ex and ek. Christ was crucified 'from' weakness and lives 'from' the power of God. The preposition marks the source: His death came about from weakness, His life springs from God's power. The apostles share that pattern 'in Him', and the power they will live by is the power that raised Him.

In verses 9 and 11 Paul uses two forms from the same family, katartisis and katartizesthe. The root idea is to put something into its right condition, the word used elsewhere of mending nets, Matthew 4:21. It describes the mending of a church that has been torn. In verse 11 it is a passive or middle imperative, so it can be read 'be mended' or 'set yourselves right.' Paul probably intends both: the church is to be restored by God, and to cooperate with that restoration. The next phrases, 'be of one mind' and 'live in peace', spell out what repair looks like. The benediction closes with koinonia, which means a sharing in common, and which here the Spirit creates.

typology.type: The two or three witnesses, Deuteronomy 19:15
typology.fulfillment: In the law the rule stops one person's word from convicting a neighbour. Paul places the visits and warnings in that frame, and the New Testament carries the idea into the church, Matthew 18:16 and 1 Timothy 5:19. The fullness comes with Christ, who says the Father and He together are two witnesses, John 8:17-18, and with the Spirit who testifies about Him, John 15:26. The type falls short in that it guards human justice, while the divine witness is not merely a safeguard against error but the very ground of salvation.

typology.type: Crucified in weakness, living by God's power
typology.fulfillment: The Servant of Isaiah is 'led like a lamb to the slaughter' and silent, Isaiah 53:7, yet God vindicates Him. The pattern of apparent defeat that turns to power runs through Joseph, David and the exiles. In Christ the pattern becomes exact: the cross is the weakest moment, and by it He is 'declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead,' Romans 1:4. Believers share the pattern, 2 Corinthians 4:10-11, though only Christ's weakness atones.

God tested Israel in the wilderness to learn what was in their heart. Here a church is told to test itself, and Paul's own apostolic ministry is tested by them. The testing finds its fullness in Christ, who passed the test that Israel failed, and in whom believers are now accepted, Romans 8:1. The type falls short because wilderness testing was a trial by law, while this examination looks for Christ in the believer as the fruit of grace.

The priests were told to bless Israel with threefold wording: bless and keep, shine and be gracious, lift up His face and give peace. Paul's closing is a threefold blessing of a different kind, and each clause names a person of the Godhead. The benediction fulfils the old one by naming the Lord Jesus as the one in whom grace is given, the Father as love's source, and the Spirit as the one who joins them. The old pattern was for a nation, while the new reaches all who are in Christ.

study.christ:
The chapter's center is verse 4, and the verse is about Christ before it is about Paul. The Corinthians had a picture of power that excluded the cross. Paul does not soften that. He says plainly that Christ was crucified in weakness. The word is the same weakness the Corinthians despised in him. By giving it to Christ, he moves the debate off the apostle and on to the Lord, and he does not retreat. The crucified one lives, and the life is the power of God. A faith that despises weakness cannot be the faith of the one who died in it.

The chapter also shows Christ as the standard of examination. The question of verse 5 is not whether the Corinthians have the right opinions or have kept the right rules. It is whether Jesus Christ is in them. The same idea runs through Paul's letters: the gospel is God's Son 'in me,' Galatians 1:16, 'Christ in you, the hope of glory,' Colossians 1:27, and Romans 8:10, 'if Christ is in you.' Because the test is Christ's presence, the answer cannot be built from self-confidence. It is received by faith and shown in a life that bears His mark.

Christ is also the speaker. The demand of verse 3 was for proof that Christ was speaking through Paul. Paul answers that the same Christ who is not weak toward them is powerful among them. Authority in the church is therefore the authority of the risen Lord working through a servant. That is why it is given 'for building you up, not for tearing you down', verse 10. The pattern is Christ's own: 'the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve,' Mark 10:45.

Finally, the benediction puts the Lord Jesus Christ first in its list. Grace is shaped like Him: 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9, a gift that cost Him everything. The love of God, shown in that gift, Romans 5:8, and the fellowship of the Spirit who unites believers to Him, complete the picture. Paul does not give the Son a lesser place. The unity of the three is assumed in the way one blessing holds them together.

We should not press the passage into more than it says. It does not give a developed doctrine of the Trinity, and the three weaknesses of verse 4 are not allegories of one another. What it gives is the pattern, the test and the blessing, all pointing to the same person.
study.god:
The passage's last verse is the nearest Paul comes to a creedal statement of the triune God in his letters, and it comes as a prayer, not a lecture. The three are named together, each with a gift: the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. They are not three moods of the same person or three rival powers. Each is named as the giver of something the Corinthians need, and the blessing is asked of all three at once. In this the doctrine of the Trinity does not float above worship; it arises out of how the church receives God.

God appears as the one whose power works through weakness. Verse 4 gives the pattern, and verse 9 gives its application: Paul rejoices to be weak if the church is strong. The God who raised the crucified Jesus is not a God who needs the apostle to look impressive. His glory is shown in raising what looked defeated. That holds the strength and the humility of God together, and it explains why Paul can say elsewhere that God's weakness is stronger than man's strength, 1 Corinthians 1:25.

God is also the God of love and peace, verse 11. These are not sentiments. In Romans 16:20 he is called the God of peace who will crush Satan under their feet, and here the title is promised to a church that is reconciling. The passage ties the presence of God to the quality of life in the congregation. A church at odds with itself cannot expect the felt nearness of the God of peace, while one that aims for harmony is promised that He will be with them.

God is truthful, too. 'We cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth,' verse 8. A God of truth does not bless a leader who builds on a lie, and He does not let a church settle for comfort in place of reality. Paul trusts the same God to settle the question of who is genuine.

For worship, the passage teaches us to end a gathering the way Paul ended the letter. We do not leave on a mere resolution to do better. We leave blessed by the Lord Jesus, the Father and the Spirit, and we greet one another as people who belong together because the three are for us.

crossReferences.note: The source of the quoted rule. It protects a person from being condemned on one voice and requires every charge to be confirmed. Paul takes it as the standard for the case he will hear at Corinth, so that nothing is decided on rumour.

Jesus applies the same rule to a brother who sins, with the two or three witnesses added at the second step. Paul's handling of Corinth follows the same order: private warning, repeated warning, then settled action.

The Lord's own answer to Paul's thorn gives the key to 13:4. His power is perfected in weakness, and Paul delights in weakness for Christ's sake. The final chapter simply states it of Christ and the apostles together.

Paul recalls how he first came to Corinth in weakness, fear and trembling, so that their faith would rest on God's power. The charge of weakness was therefore not new. He had chosen it, and it had borne fruit in the very church now judging him.

The same call to examine oneself appears in the setting of the Lord's Supper. Together the two texts show that self-examination is a regular practice of the worshipping church, aimed at repentance before the Lord's table.

Explains what it means to have Christ in you. The Spirit of God lives in the believer, and the same Spirit who raised Jesus gives life to mortal bodies. This is the positive content of the test in 2 Corinthians 13:5.
The earlier statement of the purpose of authority, for building up and not tearing down. Chapter 13:10 returns to it as the last word, tying the whole warning back to its true goal.
The psalmist asks God to search and test him. Self-examination in Scripture is a prayer, not only a task. It is asked of the one who already knows, and it leads to the way everlasting.

Paul's appeal for like-mindedness and one spirit grounds unity in encouragement in Christ, the love of God and fellowship of the Spirit. It uses the same triple pattern as the benediction and shows how fellowship produces harmony.

The baptismal formula names Father, Son and Holy Spirit under one name. It is the clearest parallel to the benediction, and the two together show that the early church thought of God as three and spoke of Him in one breath.
The God of peace is promised to crush Satan under the church's feet, with the grace of Jesus Christ following. The pairing of peace and grace in a closing prayer matches 13:11 and 13:14.
Paul says he always carries the death of Jesus in his body so that Jesus' life may be shown there. This is the practical meaning of being weak in Him yet living with Him by God's power.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a creation made for fellowship, a garden where God walked with the first man and woman. Sin broke that fellowship, and the long story that follows is of God drawing a people back. By the time of Corinth that story has reached a decisive hinge: the Son has died and risen, the Spirit has been poured out, and God is forming a church out of Jews and Gentiles. Second Corinthians shows the church as an unfinished and difficult work. It is torn by factions, proud, suspicious of its founder, and yet it is the place where God's Spirit lives.

The final chapter answers a question that has been open since the garden: how will a people who keep failing ever come to share life with a holy God? It does not say that the failure is minor. It says the answer is in Christ crucified and raised, who passed through weakness into power for them, and in a Spirit who brings them into his fellowship. The call to examine themselves belongs to the long biblical pattern in which God tests His people, as in the wilderness, Deuteronomy 8:2, and calls them to turn back, as in Lamentations 3:40. But the pattern ends differently here, because the test is no longer whether they have kept the law. It is whether Christ is in them.

The chapter also looks forward. Paul's hope is that the church will be restored, mended, and at peace. That points toward the end of the story, where God's people are made whole and the dwelling of God is with man, Revelation 21:3. The kiss of greeting and the sharing of the Spirit are small signs of that future fellowship. The apostle who warns and weeps is acting as a servant of the one who will present the church to Himself without blemish.

Finally, the closing sets the whole letter inside the life of the triune God. The Bible ends, in Revelation 22:21, on the same grace. The one story is held between two blessings, the grace given at the start in the Word made flesh, and the grace that will meet the church at the end. In between, a congregation like Corinth learns to live by the weakness and the power of Jesus, and to expect the God of love and peace to be with it.

quiz.q: On what basis does Paul say every matter will be settled when he comes?

options.text: By the testimony of two or three witnesses, drawn from the law.
options.note: Verse 1 cites the rule of witnesses from Deuteronomy.

options.text: By his own apostolic word alone, without any witnesses.
options.note: Paul deliberately invokes the standard of two or three witnesses, not his bare word.

options.text: By a vote of the whole congregation.
options.note: The passage appeals to witnesses, not to a congregational vote.

options.text: By casting lots to discover the guilty.
options.note: There is no casting of lots here; the standard is confirmed testimony.

quiz.q: What does Christ's being crucified in weakness yet living by God's power establish?

options.text: The pattern for both Paul's ministry and the believer's life, weak in Him yet living by God's power.
options.note: Verse 4 applies the pattern to us who are weak in Him.

options.text: That Christ was only appearing to be weak on the cross.
options.note: His weakness was real, yet He truly lives by God's power.

options.text: That power and weakness have nothing to do with each other.
options.note: The point is precisely that God's power works through weakness.

options.text: That believers should avoid all weakness at any cost.
options.note: Paul embraces weakness as the place where God's power is shown.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith?

options.text: Test honestly whether Jesus Christ is truly in you, leading to assurance.
options.note: Verse 5 points to the presence of Christ as the mark of genuine faith.

options.text: Count up your good works to earn a passing grade with God.
options.note: The test looks for Christ within by faith, not a tally of works.

options.text: Live in constant doubt about whether you are saved.
options.note: The aim is settled assurance, not perpetual anxiety.

options.text: Judge everyone else's faith before your own.
options.note: Paul turns the testing inward, onto yourselves.

quiz.q: What is the shape of the closing benediction?

options.text: The grace of Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit.
options.note: Verse 14 gives the fullest trinitarian blessing in Paul.

options.text: The grace of Christ alone, without the Father or the Spirit.
options.note: The blessing names all three persons together, not Christ only.

options.text: A blessing directed only to the apostles among them.
options.note: It is spoken over all of you, the whole church.

options.text: A wish for material prosperity and comfort.
options.note: The blessing is grace, love, and fellowship with the triune God, not prosperity.

questions: Paul told the Corinthians to test themselves rather than test him. When did you last honestly examine whether you are in the faith, and what did you find?
The mark of true faith is that Jesus Christ is in you. What evidences of Christ's presence and work can you actually see in your life?
Christ was crucified in weakness yet lives by God's power. How does that pattern reshape the way you view your own weakness and failure?
Paul prayed for their restoration and urged them to live in peace. Is there a broken relationship in the church or your life that God may be calling you to help mend?
The letter ends with the grace of the Son, the love of the Father, and the fellowship of the Spirit. How might dwelling on the triune God who blesses you change your worship this week?

translationNotes.note: The quotation Every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses is drawn from Deuteronomy 19:15; the BSB keeps it in quotation marks, retained here with curly quotes.
In Do you not realize that Jesus Christ is in you, unless you fail the test, the clause unless you fail the test qualifies the whole, allowing that a false profession would not stand.

The BSB footnote observes that texts vary in numbering the last verses of the chapter, and that the Byzantine text ends with Amen; the BSB numbering of verses 1 to 14 is followed here, with 13:14 as the final verse.
